segments.voice: Yesterday: Tukaram sank his notebooks in the Indrayani and sat on the bank until, tradition says, they rose dry.

Before dawn, on the stone steps that run down to the Ganges at Kashi, a young weaver lies stretched across a step in the dark. He knows a famous teacher, Ramananda, comes down here to bathe at this hour. The teacher's foot comes down on him. Startled, Ramananda cries out the name of God: Ram, Ram. And the young man goes home holding those words as if they'd been handed to him on purpose. That, tradition says, is how Kabir got his teacher.
screen: `STEPS DOWN TO THE GANGES.` → `A FOOT IN THE DARK.` → `RAM, RAM.`

segments.voice: Kabir is remembered as a weaver in Kashi, raised, tradition says, by a Muslim weaver couple, Niru and Nima, who found him as a baby by a pond. A man between worlds, who spent his life making cloth and making songs. He left a particular kind of song: the doha. A couplet, two lines that rhyme, short enough to remember after one hearing, sharp enough to keep working on you. Kabir's dohas are passed along by people singing and quoting them, and they're best taken one at a time. Today's begins, in Hindi, bura jo dekhan main chala. Roughly: I went out looking for the bad one, and couldn't find anyone. Then I searched my own heart, and found no one worse than me. Notice the trick. The first line starts on a familiar hunt: who's the problem in this office, this family, this group chat? Found nobody. The second line turns the lamp around. It doesn't say you're terrible. It says the search only works in one direction, inward, and that's where the material is. Kabir doesn't argue. He sets a little trap in two lines, and the listener walks into it and springs it. Later, when the hunt for someone to blame starts up again, the second line can come back by itself. That's what a doha is for.
screen: `A WEAVER OF KASHI.` · `THE DOHA: TWO LINES THAT RHYME.` · `I WENT LOOKING FOR THE BAD ONE.` · then, large: `I SEARCHED MY OWN HEART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've been quietly blaming lately, and let the case against them come up as it usually does. Then gently turn the lamp around and ask: what did I bring to this? Not to take all the blame, just to see your own part as clearly as you saw theirs; if you pray, you can hold what you found before God.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi whose dohas, two rhyming lines, set little traps. Today's: I went looking for the bad one, and searched my own heart.
Your line: I searched my own heart. The search only works turned inward. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: That Kabir doha about the bad one, is it saying I'm the worst person alive?
options: No, it says the hunt for who's to blame only works when you turn it inward.
No, it's mostly a joke about how hard it is to find bad people these days.
Yes, it says nobody else is ever at fault, so you should take all the blame.
chat.meaning: The doha's first line goes hunting for the bad one and finds nobody. The second turns the lamp inward, where the real work is.

Kashi.meaning: the old holy city on the Ganges, also called Varanasi

Ramananda.meaning: the famous teacher Kabir took as his guru

doha.meaning: a couplet: two rhyming lines, easy to remember

notes: The doha is paraphrased in English and only its opening words are given in Hindi transliteration, unquoted. Confirm the opening words (bura jo dekhan main chala) and that the paraphrase is fair.
The outline says 'one a day for a week' but the brief gives Kabir three days (921–923); the script says so plainly. The owner may want to adjust the title or the day count.
Birth and initiation stories (Niru and Nima, the pond, Ramananda's foot on the ghat steps) are framed as tradition. Confirm.

howItsDone mentions the Kabir Panth, Hindu devotional singing and the Guru Granth Sahib; a Keeper (and a Sikh reviewer) should confirm the phrasing. Kabir is honored by more than one community; the script tries not to claim him for any one.
